description: Comprehensive training on ladder selection, inspection, setup, safe use, and fall prevention.

slides.title: Welcome to Ladder Safety Training
slides.text: This course provides essential training on how to safely select, inspect, set up, and use ladders in the workplace. Ladder-related incidents cause thousands of injuries every year, many of which result in serious harm or lost work time. Most ladder accidents are preventable when workers follow proper procedures and remain aware of hazards. By completing this course, you will learn practical techniques that reduce risk and help ensure your safety on the job.

slides.title: Why Ladder Safety Matters
slides.text: Falls from ladders are among the leading causes of workplace injuries in construction, maintenance, and general industry. Even a short fall can result in broken bones, head injuries, or permanent disability. Many incidents occur because workers rush, use the wrong equipment, or fail to inspect the ladder before use. Understanding how accidents happen is the first step toward preventing them.

slides.title: Key Fact
slides.text: Most ladder injuries are caused by improper setup, using the wrong ladder for the task, or failing to maintain three points of contact while climbing.

slides.title: Types of Ladders
slides.text: There are several types of ladders designed for different tasks, including step ladders, extension ladders, platform ladders, and fixed ladders. Each type has specific advantages and limitations depending on the work environment and height requirements. Using the wrong ladder can create instability and increase the risk of falls. Always ensure the ladder you choose is appropriate for the job and work conditions.

slides.title: Choosing the Right Ladder
slides.text: Selecting the correct ladder involves more than just choosing the right height. You must consider weight capacity, material, and the nature of the task being performed. A ladder that is too short encourages standing on unsafe rungs, while one that cannot support your weight can fail unexpectedly. Proper selection ensures stability, safety, and efficiency while working.

slides.title: Ladder Selection Guidelines
steps: Choose a ladder rated for your weight plus tools and materials.
Select a ladder tall enough to avoid standing on top rungs.
Use fiberglass ladders when working near electricity.
Ensure the ladder meets industrial safety standards.

slides.title: Ladder Inspection
slides.text: Before every use, ladders must be carefully inspected for damage or defects. Even minor issues such as loose rungs or worn feet can lead to serious accidents. Environmental exposure, heavy use, and improper storage can weaken ladder components over time. A quick inspection can prevent equipment failure and protect workers from injury.

slides.title: Inspection Checklist
slides.text: During inspection, examine the ladder rails for cracks, bends, or corrosion that could weaken the structure. Check that all rungs are secure and free from damage, and confirm that locking mechanisms function properly. Inspect the ladder feet to ensure they provide traction and stability. If any defect is found, the ladder should not be used.

slides.title: Out of Service Rule
slides.text: Any ladder that is damaged, missing parts, or structurally compromised must be removed from service immediately and clearly marked to prevent use.

slides.title: Proper Ladder Setup
slides.text: Correct ladder placement is critical for stability and safety. Ladders should always be positioned on firm, level ground that can support both the ladder and the worker. Uneven or soft surfaces can cause shifting or tipping during use. When necessary, ladders should be secured or stabilized to prevent movement.

slides.title: Extension Ladder Angle
slides.text: Extension ladders must be positioned at the proper angle to prevent sliding or tipping. The recommended setup follows the 4-to-1 rule, meaning the base should be placed one foot away from the structure for every four feet of ladder height. This angle provides optimal balance and load distribution. Incorrect angles significantly increase the risk of accidents.

slides.title: Climbing Safely
slides.text: When climbing a ladder, always face the ladder and use both hands whenever possible. Sudden movements, distractions, or carrying objects can cause loss of balance. Climbing slowly and deliberately reduces the chance of slipping. Maintaining focus is essential while ascending or descending.

slides.title: Three Points of Contact
slides.text: Maintaining three points of contact means keeping two hands and one foot, or two feet and one hand, on the ladder at all times. This technique ensures stability and balance during climbing. If one point slips, the remaining points help prevent a fall. Workers should never compromise this rule, even for a moment.

slides.title: Electrical Hazards
slides.text: Metal ladders conduct electricity and pose a serious risk when used near power lines or electrical equipment. Contact with energized sources can result in severe injury or death. Fiberglass ladders are nonconductive and are recommended for electrical work environments. Always assess the area for electrical hazards before setting up a ladder.

slides.title: Overreaching
slides.text: Overreaching is a common cause of ladder falls. Leaning too far to one side shifts your center of gravity and can cause the ladder to tip. Instead of stretching to reach your work area, descend and reposition the ladder. Keeping your belt buckle centered between the ladder rails helps maintain balance.

slides.title: Common Causes of Falls
slides.text: Many ladder accidents occur because of unstable setup, rushing, improper equipment selection, or loss of balance. Environmental factors such as wet surfaces, wind, or poor lighting can also contribute to falls. Recognizing these hazards allows workers to take preventive action. Awareness and caution are key components of ladder safety.

slides.title: Working from a Ladder
slides.text: When performing tasks from a ladder, keep both feet on the rungs and maintain a stable stance. Avoid sudden movements that could shift your balance. Tools should be secured in a belt or raised using a rope rather than carried by hand. Proper positioning allows you to work safely and efficiently.

slides.title: Top Rung Warning
slides.text: Standing on the top rung or cap of a ladder significantly reduces stability and is one of the most common causes of falls.

slides.title: Review Section
slides.text: You will now answer several review questions to reinforce the key safety principles covered in this course.

slides.title: Final Reminder
slides.text: Safe ladder use requires proper selection, inspection, setup, and climbing technique every time you use a ladder.

slides.title: Course Complete
slides.text: Congratulations. You have completed the Ladder Safety Training course and should now understand how to reduce risks and prevent ladder-related injuries.
